setting: 01 AI-powered contract review tool for startups; asks whether charging per document reviewed triggers unauthorized practice of law concerns in specific states.
prompt: I am launching LexCheck, an AI tool that reviews startup contracts for legal risks. We plan to charge $49 per document reviewed. My co-founder Jane and I are based in Texas, but we have beta users in California and New York. We processed 1,200 documents last month with a 5% refund rate due to errors. Our monthly server costs are $3,500, and we have $85,000 in the bank. I am worried that charging a fee for analyzing legal language might be considered the unauthorized practice of law in those specific states. I need to know if our pricing model triggers regulatory red flags in California or New York specifically, and what unknown legal precedents I should research before we scale to 10,000 documents next quarter. Please outline the specific compliance risks for each state and tell me exactly which questions I must ask a qualified attorney before we launch our paid tier publicly.

setting: 02 Vertical SaaS for independent funeral homes; asks how to model unit economics when state regulations mandate a 24-month hold on pre-need funds.
prompt: We run FinalRest, a vertical SaaS platform helping independent funeral homes manage pre-need contracts. In our home state of Florida, regulations mandate that pre-need funds be held in trust for 24 months before we can recognize any revenue. We currently serve 45 funeral homes, charging $299 per month per location. Our customer acquisition cost is $1,200, and our monthly churn is 2%. We have $150,000 in operating cash and a team of six people. The hold period creates a massive gap in our unit economics modeling because we incur service costs immediately but cannot book revenue. I need help modeling our true unit economics given this 24-month regulatory hold. Specifically, I do not know how to account for the time value of money or the opportunity cost of that trapped capital in our projections. Please explain how to structure our financial model to reflect these constraints accurately and identify what specific financial metrics investors will scrutinize given this delay in revenue recognition.

setting: 03 Blockchain-based voting platform for HOAs; asks if the token distribution model classifies the software as an unregistered security under current SEC frameworks.
prompt: My company, VoteChain, provides a blockchain voting platform for Homeowners Associations. We distribute governance tokens to HOA board members to vote on community issues. We have 300 active HOAs using the system, with an average of 12 board members per HOA receiving 500 tokens each. We charge a flat setup fee of $2,000 and no monthly subscription. Our development costs were $250,000, and we have $40,000 remaining in our runway. The SEC has been aggressive lately, and I am terrified that our token distribution model classifies our software as an unregistered security. I do not know if the lack of a secondary market for these tokens protects us or if the expectation of future platform utility counts as profit expectation. I need a clear breakdown of the specific factors that might trigger security classification under current frameworks. Please list the critical unknowns regarding token utility versus investment intent that I need to resolve, and tell me precisely which legal specialists I need to consult before we onboard our next 50 HOAs.

setting: 04 Direct-to-consumer genetic testing kit for pet breeds; asks how to reserve cash for potential GDPR fines when expanding sales to European customers.
prompt: PetDNA Direct sells at-home genetic testing kits for dog breeds directly to consumers. We are expanding from the US to Germany and France next month. Each kit sells for $79, and our cost of goods sold is $22 per unit. We sold 5,000 units last quarter in the US. We have $200,000 in cash reserves. GDPR fines can reach up to 4% of global annual revenue, which scares me given our thin margins. I need a strategy to reserve cash specifically for potential GDPR fines or data breach penalties when handling European customer data. I do not know what percentage of our projected European revenue is standard to set aside for compliance contingencies or if there is a fixed cap I should aim for. Please explain how to calculate an appropriate reserve fund based on our volume and risk profile. Also, identify the specific data processing activities that carry the highest fines so I can prioritize our audit efforts and know exactly when to hire a European data protection officer.

setting: 05 Autonomous last-mile delivery bot for university campuses; asks whether local municipal ordinances require a commercial driver's license for the remote operators.
prompt: CampusBot operates autonomous last-mile delivery bots on university campuses. We currently deploy 50 bots across three campuses in Ohio. Each bot costs $4,000 to manufacture, and we charge universities $1.50 per delivery. We average 200 deliveries per bot daily. Our remote operations center has four staff members monitoring the fleet. We have $120,000 in the bank. Some local municipal ordinances in cities like Columbus seem to require a commercial driver's license for anyone remotely supervising autonomous vehicles, even if they never touch the wheel. I am unsure if our current monitoring staff needs CDLs under these specific local laws or if an exemption exists for low-speed campus zones. I need to understand the licensing requirements for our remote operators in these municipalities. Please clarify the regulatory landscape regarding remote supervision licenses and highlight the unknown penalties we face if we are non-compliant. Tell me which specific municipal codes I need to review and when I must engage a local traffic attorney to avoid shutting down our fleet.

setting: 06 Cloud-based payroll processor for gig economy platforms; asks how to calculate withholding liabilities when workers operate across three different tax jurisdictions.
prompt: GigPay is a cloud-based payroll processor designed for gig economy platforms. We currently process payments for 12,000 workers who operate across California, New York, and Texas simultaneously. Our fee is 1.5% of total payroll volume. Last month, we processed $4.5 million in payments. Our operating expenses are $60,000 per month, and we have $300,000 in cash. Calculating withholding liabilities is a nightmare because workers often cross state lines within a single pay period, triggering different tax rates and thresholds. I do not know how to accurately calculate the pro-rated withholding liabilities when a worker earns income in three different jurisdictions in one week. I need a method to determine the correct tax withholdings without over-reserving cash or facing penalties. Please explain the mechanics of multi-jurisdiction withholding for gig workers and identify the specific unknown variables in current interstate tax compacts that could affect our liability. Tell me exactly what data points I need to collect from workers and which tax professionals I need to retain to validate our algorithm.

setting: 07 Tele-psychiatry network connecting patients to out-of-state doctors; asks what malpractice insurance coverage is needed to comply with interstate licensure compacts.
prompt: MindLink is a tele-psychiatry network connecting patients in rural areas to doctors licensed in other states. We have 200 doctors and 3,500 active patients. We charge patients $120 per session and pay doctors $80. Our monthly platform costs are $15,000, and we have $90,000 in runway. We are expanding to states participating in the interstate licensure compact, but I am unclear on the malpractice insurance requirements. Do we need a single national policy, or does each doctor need specific coverage extensions for every state they treat patients in? I do not know if the compact simplifies insurance requirements or if it only handles licensing. I need to understand the exact malpractice coverage needed to comply with these compacts and avoid gaps in liability. Please outline the insurance structures required for interstate telehealth and highlight the unknown risks if a doctor treats a patient in a non-compact state by accident. Tell me which specific insurance brokers specialize in tele-psychiatry and what questions I must ask them before our next expansion wave.

setting: 08 Smart water meter manufacturer for municipal utilities; asks whether offering a revenue-share model violates state laws regarding public infrastructure privatization.
prompt: AquaSmart manufactures smart water meters for municipal utilities. We are proposing a new revenue-share model where we install meters for free and take 10% of the water savings detected for five years. Our hardware cost is $150 per unit, and we have pilots in two cities in Arizona. We have $500,000 in funding and a team of ten. However, I am concerned that offering a revenue-share model based on public utility savings might violate state laws regarding the privatization of public infrastructure. I do not know if Arizona or neighboring states have specific statutes prohibiting private entities from profiting directly from municipal utility efficiency gains. I need to determine if our business model is legally viable or if it triggers anti-privatization clauses. Please analyze the potential legal conflicts with state public utility codes and identify the unknown regulatory hurdles we might face during city council approvals. Tell me exactly which legal arguments municipalities use to reject such models and which attorneys I need to consult to structure a compliant agreement.

setting: 09 Digital asset inheritance vault for crypto holders; asks how to structure the service to avoid being classified as a money transmitter requiring state bonds.
prompt: CryptoWill is a digital asset inheritance vault that allows crypto holders to designate beneficiaries for their wallets upon death. We charge a flat annual fee of $50 per vault. We have 8,000 active users and $400,000 in annual recurring revenue. Our server and security costs are $100,000 per year, and we have $250,000 in the bank. Several states require money transmitters to post surety bonds if they hold or facilitate the transfer of value. I am trying to structure our service so that we never touch the private keys directly, but I do not know if facilitating the automated transfer of assets upon a death certificate verification classifies us as a money transmitter requiring state bonds. I need to understand how to structure the technical workflow to avoid this classification. Please explain the regulatory triggers for money transmitter laws in this context and identify the unknown legal interpretations of 'custody' in inheritance scenarios. Tell me which specific states have the strictest definitions and which legal experts I should hire to draft our terms of service safely.

setting: 10 AI-driven medical coding assistant for rural clinics; asks if billing insurers based on algorithmic suggestions creates liability for upcoding audits.
prompt: CodeAssist is an AI-driven medical coding assistant for rural clinics. We charge clinics $500 per month per provider. We have 40 clinics using our tool, covering 120 doctors. Our development costs are $20,000 monthly, and we have $180,000 in cash. The AI suggests billing codes based on doctor notes, but if the AI suggests a higher code than justified, it could look like upcoding. I am worried that billing insurers based on algorithmic suggestions creates liability for us if audits find systematic upcoding. I do not know if the clinic or our software company bears the legal responsibility for AI-suggested errors in billing submissions. I need to understand the liability landscape for AI-assisted medical coding and audit risks. Please explain who typically holds liability in these scenarios and what unknown precedents exist for algorithmic billing errors. Tell me exactly what compliance safeguards I must build into the product to protect against audits and which healthcare attorneys I need to consult before we sign our next large hospital group contract.
